interview_metadata.name: Milton Wells
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Well, I was born and raised right here in Oklahoma City, over on the northwest side before it spread out the way it has now. My folks were steady, churchgoing people, not fancy, but we always had what we needed. My dad worked with his hands, and my mother kept the house running and later did office work, so I learned early that if something broke, you studied it, took it apart carefully, and fixed it if you could. I finished high school and went straight into work. College was not really in the cards for me; I wanted a paycheck, and I liked practical work. I became a handyman over time, doing carpentry, plumbing repairs, small engine work, hanging doors, fixing leaky sinks, building decks, that kind of thing. I married in my twenties, had two children, and tried to be a good provider. The marriage lasted a long while, but it got strained, especially with money worries and me being gone on jobs or tired when I came home. We divorced years back. That was painful, but we stayed civil for the children. Now I am retired, live alone, and spend my week with the senior center, church outreach, gardening, fishing, photography, and trying to write down some of my life before the little details slip away.

follow_ups.question: What are your clearest memories from childhood in Oklahoma City?
follow_ups.response: Summer evenings mostly. We would sit outside after supper because the house was hot, and the men in the neighborhood would talk about work while the kids rode bikes until dark. I remember church potlucks, mowing lawns for pocket money, and my father showing me how to sharpen a hand saw.

follow_ups.question: What did you like most about handyman work?
follow_ups.response: I liked that the problem was right in front of you. A pipe leaked, a hinge sagged, a mower would not start, and you had to use your head and hands together. I also liked helping widows and older folks who were nervous about being overcharged.

follow_ups.question: How has retirement changed your sense of who you are?
follow_ups.response: At first it left a hole, because I was used to being needed. Then the senior center asked me to teach small home-repair workshops, and that gave me purpose again. I still feel like a working man, just working for the community now.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: One crossroads was after high school. A counselor told me I might try community college, but my father knew a contractor who needed a helper. I chose work. I sometimes wonder what would have happened if I had studied drafting or business, but that first job taught me tools, job sites, and how to deal with customers. Another crossroads came after my divorce. I could have pulled back and become bitter, and for a while I was close to that. Instead, my pastor asked me to help repair a ramp for an older church member, and that led to more volunteer work. That decision helped me turn a hard season into service.

follow_ups.question: Who influenced you most at that first crossroads?
follow_ups.response: My father. He did not push hard, but he believed a man ought to earn and learn a trade. I respected that.

follow_ups.question: What did the volunteer ramp project change for you?
follow_ups.response: It reminded me that my skills still mattered even if my home life had changed. The woman sent me a thank-you card, and I kept it in my toolbox for years.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: The work decision mostly felt practical, like the next right step. The choice after my divorce was more conscious. I remember deciding I did not want to spend my older years complaining.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk that decision over with anyone?
follow_ups.response: I talked with my pastor and one friend at the senior center. Mostly they listened and reminded me to keep showing up.

follow_ups.question: What did you do first after making that decision?
follow_ups.response: I signed up for a Saturday church repair day and then agreed to teach a basic tool safety class.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes, especially during the divorce. Counseling probably would have helped us earlier, but we were stubborn and old-fashioned about private problems. For work, I think trade-school guidance would have been useful.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have felt acceptable to you then?
follow_ups.response: Something practical and private. I would have gone to a marriage class or a financial planning session before I would have called it counseling.

follow_ups.question: Do you offer that kind of help now?
follow_ups.response: I try to. When younger volunteers are struggling, I tell them to ask for help before pride makes the bill bigger.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am divorced and not living with a partner. I have two grown children. My daughter, Karen, lives in Edmond and works in a school office. She checks on me by phone two or three times a week and usually comes by on Sunday afternoon if her schedule allows. My son, Brian, is down near Norman and works around auto parts and repairs. We talk less often, maybe every couple of weeks, but when we get together we can spend a whole afternoon talking engines or football. I have three grandchildren, two teenagers and one younger one. I am not the grandpa who buys the flashiest gifts, but I show up for birthdays, help with little repairs, and sometimes take them fishing if they are willing to get up early.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Karen usually do when she visits?
follow_ups.response: She looks over my mail pile because I misplace receipts, and then we drink coffee. Sometimes I send her home with tomatoes or jars of stew.

follow_ups.question: How do you stay connected with your grandchildren?
follow_ups.response: Texts mostly, though I am slow at typing. I also mail birthday cards with a little cash because I still like doing that the old way.

follow_ups.question: Are you dating or interested in another relationship?
follow_ups.response: No, not really. I have lady friends at church and the senior center, but I am settled living by myself.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My ex-wife, Linda, is still in the picture because of the children and grandkids. We are polite and can sit at the same birthday table, but we do not spend time together otherwise.

follow_ups.question: Do you coordinate holidays with her?
follow_ups.response: Yes, usually through Karen. Thanksgiving is sometimes split, and Christmas depends on who can host.

follow_ups.question: Do you have siblings?
follow_ups.response: I had one older brother, Ray, but he passed several years ago. I still talk with his widow around Christmas.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yes. I have a few close friends from the senior center. Earl and I play chess on Tuesdays and argue about the Cowboys. Sam fishes with me at Lake Hefner or Arcadia when the weather is decent. At church, I am close with Pastor Jim and a woman named Marlene who organizes the outreach pantry. Those people notice if I miss a week, and that matters.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see Earl and Sam?
follow_ups.response: Earl most Tuesdays, unless one of us has a doctor appointment. Sam and I fish maybe twice a month in warm weather.

follow_ups.question: What makes someone a close friend to you?
follow_ups.response: Reliability. I do not need constant talk, but if a person says they will be there at seven, they ought to be there.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in northwest Oklahoma City, in the 73132 area. It is mostly older houses, some rentals, some longtime owners like me. You see pickup trucks, kids on bikes, people walking dogs, and a few yards that are kept real nice next to yards that need attention. I like being close enough to the senior center, church, grocery store, and Lake Hefner. It is not fancy, but it is familiar. The wind can really whip through, and in spring everybody keeps one eye on the weather.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few. I wave at most of them, and I help Mrs. Alvarez next door with her hose bib and trash bins.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often nearby?
follow_ups.response: The senior center, Crest grocery, church, and the lake. I plan errands in a loop to save gas.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I lock my doors, keep porch lights working, and do not leave tools visible in the truck. There have been car break-ins around, but I do not feel afraid in my own home.

follow_ups.question: Do you walk in the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Some mornings, but I prefer the senior center walking club because the path is even and there are people around.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed any habits because of safety concerns?
follow_ups.response: I installed a better motion light and stopped leaving my fishing tackle in the garage with the door open.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is convenience and knowing the rhythms of the place. The downside is traffic, storm season, and watching some properties get neglected. Still, I would rather be here than start over somewhere unfamiliar.

follow_ups.question: What would you improve if you could?
follow_ups.response: Sidewalks and drainage. After a hard rain, certain corners hold water too long.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you rooted there?
follow_ups.response: Church, family nearby, and memories. I know which store has good tomatoes and which roads to avoid at five o'clock.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live by myself. It is a small house, and I keep one bedroom as a sort of office and model-building room. My daughter has a key, and one grandson has stayed overnight before a fishing trip, but nobody lives here with me. I like quiet mornings and having my tools where I left them, though I do admit I still misplace receipts.

follow_ups.question: Do you prefer living alone?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I like company, but I also like deciding when the television is on and when the house is quiet.

follow_ups.question: Who would help if you had an emergency at home?
follow_ups.response: Karen first, then my neighbor Mrs. Alvarez, and Pastor Jim if it was something bigger.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It is just me permanently.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been that way for years.

follow_ups.question: Do visitors keep belongings there?
follow_ups.response: No, just a spare toothbrush for grandkids.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: A grandchild may stay one night before fishing, but that is occasional.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe three or four times a year.

follow_ups.question: Where do they sleep?
follow_ups.response: On the guest bed in the room with my model cars.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: Any family temporarily away who still uses your address?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any mail for others coming there?
follow_ups.response: Only occasional old mail for my son, and I forward it.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: I am up around 6:00 most mornings. Monday is usually errands, bills, and garden work. Tuesday I go to the senior center for walking club and chess. Wednesday I often help with a repair workshop or church outreach planning. Thursday is quieter: laundry, reading, photo sorting on the computer. Friday I may fish early if weather allows. Saturday depends on family or volunteer events. Sunday is church, lunch, and sometimes Karen stops by.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 9:30. If the Thunder are playing late, I might stretch it, but I pay for it the next day.

follow_ups.question: What is the first thing you do in the morning?
follow_ups.response: Start coffee, check the weather, and step outside to look at the garden.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I do not work for pay now. I am retired from handyman work. What I do resembles work, though: I lead senior-center workshops on simple plumbing fixes, basic carpentry, and tool safety. I also coordinate volunteers for church repair days, keeping sign-up sheets and supply lists. That is usually a few hours a week, more if an event is coming up.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever take paid repair jobs anymore?
follow_ups.response: Very rarely, and only for someone I know. I do not advertise and I do not climb ladders like I used to.

follow_ups.question: What workshop did you teach most recently?
follow_ups.response: How to shut off water, replace a flapper, and use plumber's tape without making a mess.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep the church outreach tool inventory on a spreadsheet, and I balance a small volunteer account with receipts. I tend my vegetable garden most days, though I am guilty of over-watering the lettuce. I also call one older church member, Mr. Haney, every Thursday because he is mostly homebound.

follow_ups.question: What do you grow in the garden?
follow_ups.response: Tomatoes, peppers, lettuce, green beans, and a few flowers for color.

follow_ups.question: How do you organize the volunteer account?
follow_ups.response: I keep receipts in envelopes by month, then enter them into a simple spreadsheet. When I do not misplace the envelope, it works fine.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: I have started walking more regularly because my doctor wants me moving for blood pressure and knees. I also cut back on evening activities. I used to go to more high-school football games, but early evening fatigue catches me now, especially after a busy day. I do more morning things and fewer night things.

follow_ups.question: When did you make that change?
follow_ups.response: Over the past year, after a checkup where my doctor was plain with me about staying active.

follow_ups.question: Do you miss evening events?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but I would rather be steady the next morning than prove something at night.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are grown, so there is no school-year routine for them now. When they were young, Linda handled more of the school mornings because I left early for jobs. These days I hear about the grandkids' schedules: school, band for one, soccer for another, and a lot of homework on laptops.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with grandchild transportation?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally, if Karen asks and it is daytime. I avoid night driving when I can.

follow_ups.question: What activities do you most enjoy attending?
follow_ups.response: Band concerts are easier for me than sports because they are seated and predictable.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My own experiences have been limited. I have had a couple traffic stops over the years, mostly warnings, and once I called police when tools were stolen from a shed. I try to be respectful and keep things calm. I know not everybody has the same experience, but mine personally have been ordinary.

follow_ups.question: What happened with the stolen tools?
follow_ups.response: They took a report, but I never got the tools back. After that I improved the lock and lighting.

follow_ups.question: Do you know officers personally?
follow_ups.response: One retired officer comes to the senior center sometimes. We talk more about fishing than police work.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Storm traffic control stands out. After bad weather, officers directing intersections can make a real difference. I also remember school resource officers from when my grandchildren were younger.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever filed a complaint or had a conflict with police?
follow_ups.response: No, I have not.

follow_ups.question: Do you follow local policing news?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat, mostly through local news and conversations at church.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I had a nephew who got a DUI years ago, and that shook the family. He did the classes, paid the fines, and thankfully got himself straightened out.

follow_ups.question: Did that change how your family talked about alcohol?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially around driving after gatherings. Nobody wanted to repeat that.

follow_ups.question: Did you help him during that period?
follow_ups.response: I gave him rides to work a few times and told him straight that trust takes time to rebuild.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly, especially in presidential and governor races, and I try to vote in local elections too. I was raised that voting is part of citizenship. I do not put signs all over my yard, but I read the sample ballot, check the judges and local questions, and go early if I can.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote in person or by mail?
follow_ups.response: Usually in person, early in the day. I like getting it done.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk politics with?
follow_ups.response: A little with Earl, my son, and a couple church friends. I avoid heated arguments.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself a conservative-leaning Republican, but not a loud one. I believe in personal responsibility, balanced budgets, respect for police and military, and keeping government from wasting money. At the same time, I believe communities have obligations. If an elderly person needs food or a family gets hit by a tornado, you help. I am more practical than ideological. I do not like cruelty in politics, and I get tired of everyone acting like the other side is evil. On local issues, I care about roads, schools being run sensibly, public safety, and whether tax money is accounted for. My faith shapes me some, but I do not think politics should replace church or family.

follow_ups.question: Have you always identified as Republican?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, yes. My family leaned that way, though older Oklahoma politics had more conservative Democrats than people remember.

follow_ups.question: Are there issues where you differ from many Republicans?
follow_ups.response: I am more open to practical health-care help for working families and seniors. I do not like waste, but I know people can work hard and still need help.

follow_ups.question: What political style turns you off?
follow_ups.response: Mocking people, name-calling, and acting like compromise is weakness. That wears me out.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become less trusting of cable-news shouting and more interested in local facts. Age does that maybe. When you are dealing with roads, clinics, and senior services, slogans do not fix much. I am still conservative, but I have softened on some social issues because I have met more people through volunteer work and realized life is complicated.

follow_ups.question: What changed your mind most?
follow_ups.response: Knowing real people instead of categories. At the pantry, you meet folks who do not fit neat political boxes.

follow_ups.question: Where do you still feel firm?
follow_ups.response: Fiscal responsibility and personal accountability. Those still matter to me.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I would say somewhat. I did not march or put signs out, but I listened more than I used to. As a white man my age, I know I grew up not having to think about some things other people deal with. I still believe most police are trying to do a hard job, but I also believe bad treatment should be taken seriously.

follow_ups.question: What made you listen more?
follow_ups.response: Conversations at church and seeing younger people in my family talk about it with real concern.

follow_ups.question: Did it change any behavior?
follow_ups.response: Mostly it made me slower to dismiss someone's story just because it differs from mine.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the basic issue is whether people are treated fairly and whether government power is accountable. I may not agree with every slogan or tactic, but I understand why people want answers when someone dies in custody or during a police encounter. I also worry about communities losing trust, because without trust, even good officers have a harder job.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss this at church?
follow_ups.response: A little, usually carefully. Our pastor tries to keep people listening rather than arguing.

follow_ups.question: What would accountability look like to you?
follow_ups.response: Clear investigations, body cameras used properly, and discipline when someone abuses authority.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the country has made progress, but we are not finished. Growing up, I heard comments that people would not say out loud now, and some of that thinking did damage. I try to judge people by character and conduct, but I also understand history leaves marks. My grandkids are more direct about these conversations than my generation was.

follow_ups.question: Do you remember race being discussed when you were young?
follow_ups.response: Not honestly. Adults mostly avoided it or spoke in coded ways.

follow_ups.question: What do you learn from your grandchildren on this?
follow_ups.response: They are quicker to call something unfair. Sometimes I think they are too quick, but often they see things I missed.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked with family and church friends. I have not joined protests. My response has been to listen, ask questions, and try not to make every conversation a debate.

follow_ups.question: Who have you talked with most?
follow_ups.response: Karen and one younger volunteer at church who sees things differently than I do.

follow_ups.question: Have those talks been tense?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but they stay respectful if we keep our voices down.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: It varies. Earl thinks the whole thing is overblown and changes the subject. Karen is more concerned and wants reforms. My son is more law-and-order but still thinks body cameras are useful. At church, people are mixed, so we try to focus on treating neighbors decently.

follow_ups.question: Does disagreement affect your relationships?
follow_ups.response: Not much. We have known each other too long to throw a friendship away over one subject.

follow_ups.question: Who has influenced you most?
follow_ups.response: Probably Karen. She has a calm way of explaining why something matters.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: For 73, I am doing all right. I have controlled high blood pressure, some arthritis in my knees and hands, and I get tired earlier in the evening than I used to. I take a blood pressure pill, try to walk, and keep up with checkups. My hearing is not perfect, but I manage. I am grateful I can still garden, fish, and teach workshops.

follow_ups.question: What limits you the most day to day?
follow_ups.response: Knees on stairs and long standing. I plan breaks now.

follow_ups.question: How do you track medications?
follow_ups.response: A weekly pill box beside the coffee maker. Morning routines help.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Routine makes it easier. If I walk in the morning and cook at home, I do better. What makes it hard is liking fried catfish, cornbread, and strong coffee, and sometimes skipping stretching when I feel stiff. Weather also matters; icy days keep me inside.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit are you most consistent about?
follow_ups.response: Walking club on Tuesdays and checking my blood pressure at home.

follow_ups.question: What food is hardest to moderate?
follow_ups.response: Fried catfish. I can pass up sweets easier than good catfish.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: No major diagnosis, thank goodness. My doctor adjusted my blood pressure medicine last year, and I had a knee arthritis flare after overdoing garden work. I also had cataract checks, but no surgery yet. The biggest change is accepting that I cannot work like I am forty-five.

follow_ups.question: What happened with the knee flare?
follow_ups.response: I spent too long kneeling while setting tomato cages. It swelled, and I used ice, rest, and a brace for a week.

follow_ups.question: Do you use assistive devices?
follow_ups.response: A folding garden stool and sometimes a knee brace. I am not too proud for those.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: They affect my pace more than my independence. I avoid ladders, heavy lifting, and night driving when I can. I can still care for myself and help others, but I choose tasks more carefully.

follow_ups.question: Have you turned down volunteer tasks because of health?
follow_ups.response: Yes, roof work and hauling heavy lumber. I will organize the crew instead.

follow_ups.question: Does that bother you?
follow_ups.response: Some. A man used to doing things has to learn to delegate.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes. My daughter had a scare with high blood sugar and had to change diet and exercise. My ex-wife has had some back trouble. I also check on older church members who are dealing with worse than I am. At this age, health is part of nearly every conversation.

follow_ups.question: Do you help Karen with her health changes?
follow_ups.response: Mostly by not tempting her with too much cornbread and by walking with her when she visits.

follow_ups.question: Does caregiving stress you?
follow_ups.response: A little, but practical help calms me. If I can drive someone or fix a grab bar, I feel useful.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: Medicare helps a lot, and I have a supplemental plan I budget for. Appointments can take time, and specialist visits are not cheap, but I have not had to skip necessary care recently. Years ago, before retirement, I delayed dental work because money was tight. These days I plan ahead and ask questions before agreeing to anything expensive.

follow_ups.question: How do you choose doctors?
follow_ups.response: Recommendations from my primary doctor, church friends, and whether the office is within a reasonable drive.

follow_ups.question: What health cost worries you most?
follow_ups.response: Dental and hearing aids. Those can sneak up on a person.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing formal like that. I use home remedies in the ordinary Oklahoma way: heating pad, ice pack, Epsom salt soak, honey and lemon for a cough. My mother believed in Vicks for nearly everything. But for real medical trouble, I go to the doctor.

follow_ups.question: Do you take supplements?
follow_ups.response: A basic multivitamin and sometimes fish oil, but I tell my doctor.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you those home remedies?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my mother and older church ladies.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I quit cigarettes decades ago when the kids were little. I drink very little, maybe a beer during a Cowboys game or at a family cookout, but not as a coping habit. When I am stressed, I go outside, work on a model car, or drive to the lake.

follow_ups.question: What helped you quit smoking?
follow_ups.response: Linda hated the smell, and I knew it was bad for the kids. I quit rough, but I quit.

follow_ups.question: What do you do first when stress hits?
follow_ups.response: I make coffee, step outside, and find something small to fix.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I take prescribed blood pressure medicine as directed. For pain, I use over-the-counter acetaminophen now and then, especially after gardening. I do not use marijuana or other substances. The most recent was probably two tablets after my knee acted up last weekend.

follow_ups.question: Are you concerned about pain medicine?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I am cautious. I saw enough people get tangled up with stronger pills after injuries.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever skip prescriptions?
follow_ups.response: No, not intentionally. The pill box keeps me honest.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I pay through Medicare, my supplemental premium, and regular budgeting. I keep a medical folder with statements, though sometimes receipts wander off. Karen has insurance through work. We compare notes on costs, and I remind everyone to use preventive appointments because catching things early is cheaper and better.

follow_ups.question: Do medical bills strain your monthly budget?
follow_ups.response: They can, but I plan for premiums and prescriptions. Surprise dental work is harder.

follow_ups.question: Who helps with paperwork?
follow_ups.response: Karen helps if something looks confusing.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally pro-vaccine. I get flu shots and COVID boosters when my doctor recommends them. At my age, I do not see much wisdom in taking unnecessary risks.

follow_ups.question: Did you have concerns about side effects?

follow_ups.question: Do you use the internet for health questions?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but carefully. I prefer official sites and then confirm with a professional.

follow_ups.question: Who is your most trusted person source?

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.

Karen noticed I was short on the phone and came by with soup. The next week I went back just to sit in on chess, and Earl made a joke about me being rusty. That helped more than I expected.

follow_ups.question: Did you tell anyone you were struggling?
follow_ups.response: Not directly. Karen read between the lines.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from that stretch?

transcript.response: I would not say I have clinical depression, but I have had low moods, especially after the divorce and sometimes in winter. I worry, but I am not an anxious person day to day. I cope with routine, prayer, talking to people I trust, and keeping my hands busy.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever sought counseling?
follow_ups.response: No formal counseling, though looking back it might have helped.

follow_ups.question: What signs tell you a low mood is coming?
follow_ups.response: I stop answering calls quickly and let dishes or mail pile up.

I like hymns and old country gospel, and at church socials somebody usually plays Merle Haggard or similar music. I am not perfect, but church gives my week shape and keeps me connected.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.

transcript.response: I do not use social media that way personally. If I need support, I call family, church, or a friend. I will respond to others' prayer requests or meal trains online, though.

follow_ups.response: No, not unless it was for a church cause, and even then I would prefer proper channels.

follow_ups.question: What online support do you give others?

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: I was a handyman and maintenance repairman. The work included carpentry, plumbing repairs, doors, trim, drywall patches, fence repairs, decks, small engine troubleshooting, and general home maintenance. The important duties were diagnosing the problem, estimating materials, doing the work safely, and treating customers honestly. A lot of the job was communication: explaining what needed fixing, what could wait, and what was beyond my license or ability. I learned to keep notes, receipts, and a clean truck because disorder costs money.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: She worked as an office clerk and receptionist. She answered phones, typed invoices, filed papers, greeted customers, and kept records straight. She was organized in a way I still admire.

follow_ups.question: Did you learn record-keeping from her?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she believed every bill had a place.

follow_ups.question: Was she proud of that work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, quietly proud.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: She worked for a local insurance and real estate office for a good while. They handled policies, property paperwork, and customer accounts. It was a small office where everyone knew everybody's business.

follow_ups.question: Was it close to home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a short drive.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit her there?
follow_ups.response: A few times, and I remember the smell of paper and coffee.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, he worked steadily.

follow_ups.question: Was he the main earner?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when we were young.

follow_ups.question: Did he ever have long unemployment?
follow_ups.response: No, not that I remember.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: He worked maintenance for a manufacturing warehouse. He repaired equipment, kept machinery running, handled basic electrical and mechanical issues, and made sure the building did not fall behind. He brought home the habit of fixing before replacing.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you tools?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly by making me watch first and touch second.

follow_ups.question: What did he emphasize?
follow_ups.response: Safety, patience, and putting tools back.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: It was a warehouse and light manufacturing operation tied to farm and industrial supplies. They stored parts, assembled some equipment, and shipped goods around the region. It was practical, noisy, and full of men who knew machines.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever consider working there?
follow_ups.response: Briefly, but I ended up with a contractor instead.

follow_ups.question: How did that place shape him?
follow_ups.response: It made him steady and exacting. He hated waste.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: I hope to stay healthy enough to live independently, keep my house in good order, and keep serving without becoming foolish about my limits. I want to continue the senior-center workshops and mentor younger volunteers who have never learned basic repairs. I would like to finish at least a rough memoir for my children and grandchildren, with photos from Oklahoma prairies, Sedona, the Flint Hills, and maybe someday the Grand Canyon at sunrise. I hope my family stays close even if everyone is busy. Mostly I hope to be useful, steady, and at peace with the life I have lived.

follow_ups.question: What would make the memoir feel finished?
follow_ups.response: A chapter for each season of life, a few lessons learned, and photos labeled so the grandkids know the stories.

follow_ups.question: What would you need for the Grand Canyon trip?
follow_ups.response: Good health, careful budget, motel reservations, and someone knowing my route each day.

follow_ups.question: What do you fear losing most?
follow_ups.response: Independence and usefulness.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: Faith, family, usefulness, honesty, and keeping your word. I value modest living and doing good work whether anybody applauds or not. I value old friends, quiet mornings, a well-kept tool, a garden tomato, and the chance to help someone who cannot repay you. At this age, you realize reputation is built in small daily choices.

follow_ups.question: Which value did your parents teach most strongly?
follow_ups.response: Keep your word. If you say you will do something, do it.

follow_ups.question: Which value do you hope your grandchildren remember?
follow_ups.response: Usefulness with kindness. Skills matter more when they serve people.
